# Infinite vs Column: who runs the compliance program


Column is a nationally chartered bank with serious rails — US payments, SWIFT, FX — that fintechs build on directly. Infinite operates a different layer: a stablecoin-native compliance network where the accounts, the fiat and stablecoin rails, and the compliance program itself are run for you. The practical difference is who does the regulated work. On a platform bank, your team builds and runs it; on Infinite, the network does.


By[Nikhil Srinivasan](https://infinite.net/company/about) , Founder & CEO


·


Last updated Aug 10, 2026

TL;DR


## Key takeaways


1. Column is a nationally chartered bank that built its own core and connects directly to the Federal Reserve.
2. Column's public documentation makes customers responsible for KYC and KYB under their own documented CIP and BSA/AML policies, which Column periodically reviews.
3. Infinite is not a bank; it operates a compliance network above chartered partner banks where every customer gets a real demand deposit account.
4. On Infinite, KYC, KYB, sanctions screening, and ongoing transaction monitoring run under the network's compliance program, not the customer's.
5. Column's public product documentation lists no stablecoin or digital-asset products, while stablecoins sit natively in every Infinite Account.


01


## A chartered bank and a compliance network


Column earned its reputation the hard way: it owns a national bank charter, built its own core with no middleware, connects directly to the Federal Reserve, and runs real international rails. Some of the best fintechs in the world build on it. If the comparison were about rails, there would be no essay to write.


The comparison is about operating models. Infinite is not a bank and does not sell bank access — it operates a[compliance network](https://infinite.net/funds-flow/third-party) above chartered, FDIC-insured partner banks, where every customer gets a real demand deposit account and the compliance program that governs the money is part of the product, not a prerequisite for it.


02


## Who runs the compliance program


Column's public documentation is explicit about the split: its customers are responsible for running KYC and KYB on every entity they bring, with their own documented CIP and BSA/AML policies, and Column periodically reviews that work. That model gives sophisticated programs control — and it means the compliance program is yours to build and answer for before the first account opens.


On Infinite, the program ships with the account. KYC, KYB, sanctions screening, and ongoing transaction monitoring run under Infinite's compliance program, through[hosted flows that carry your brand](https://infinite.net/compliance/embedded) .[AI assembles each case and a named analyst signs every decision](https://infinite.net/compliance/ai) , so first-time reviews that traditionally take around 30 days close in 1–2. And because verification status travels with the counterparty, a business vetted once is vetted for every business on the network.


> The scarce thing is not a bank account or a rail. It is a compliance program that scales with other people's money.


This is what moving third-party money actually requires. When the funds belong to your customers, regulators expect customer-level diligence on every one of them — not just on your platform. On a platform bank, that diligence program is your project. On Infinite,[it is the design center](https://infinite.net/funds-flow/third-party) : onboarding, screening, and portfolio-wide monitoring run on the network and are documented for your auditors.


03


## Stablecoins are native, not adjacent


As of this writing, Column's public product documentation lists no stablecoin or digital-asset products. On Infinite, stablecoins are not a category beside the account — they are in it: USDC, USDT, OUSD, and USDG sit next to fiat balances,[dollars convert by native mint and burn](https://infinite.net/payments/stablecoins) with no intermediary liquidity providers, transfers settle in minutes around the clock, and corridors are funded just in time instead of pre-funded a week ahead. FX runs across GBP, EUR, MXN, and BRL with firm, all-in quotes, with additional corridors — including AED and INR — being added.


04


## When a platform bank is the right choice


If you are a fintech with a licensed, staffed compliance program that wants a direct relationship at the charter layer, a platform bank like Column is a genuinely strong answer — that is its lane. The fork comes when the regulated work is the part you don't want to rebuild: when you want every customer to hold a real account, stablecoins to sit natively beside fiat, and the compliance program — onboarding, RFIs, monitoring, audit trail — to be operated for you rather than by you. That is the job[Infinite](https://infinite.net/platform/managed-account) is built for.


FAQ


## Frequently asked questions


### How is Infinite different from building on a platform bank?


A platform bank gives you accounts and rails; the compliance program — CIP, BSA/AML policies, KYC/KYB execution — is typically yours to build and run, subject to the bank's review. Infinite operates that program as part of the product: verification, screening, monitoring, and RFIs run on the network, in your brand, documented for your auditors.


### Does Infinite support stablecoins and fiat in the same account?


Yes. Each Infinite Account holds USDC, USDT, OUSD, and USDG beside fiat balances, with conversion by native mint and burn inside the network — no exchange accounts or intermediary liquidity providers — and stablecoin transfers that settle in minutes, 24/7, including weekends and holidays.


### Can my platform move money for its own customers on Infinite?


Yes — third-party flows are the design center, not an exception. Each of your customers gets a real demand deposit account established under Infinite's partner banks, onboarded through whitelabel flows, with screening and monitoring run across your whole program by the network rather than by your team.
